description:
✋ Raise your hand if you’ve read an entire page of a book and absorbed exactly none of it.

We blame our focus. Or our discipline. Or the book.

Jim Kwik (@jimkwik) is a top brain coach and has spent 34 years teaching people how to actually learn. And he thinks every book on your nightstand is still salvageable.

What’s the last book you actually finished?

🎧 Listen to the full episode of A Bit of Optimism wherever you get your podcasts.
transcript: I buy books like they're going out of fashion and I've started a lot of books and I can't finish them. And my ADHD, I get very distracted or I'm like, oh, I'll read, but then I don't. And I have the books piled up next to my bed. Literally, I have a pile of books next to my bed that don't get read, right? So for somebody with my funny brain, the ADHD brain, can you give me some tips or tricks to make me feel like I'm making progress on enjoying myself, so then I'll go back and do more of it. I would say a visual pacer could help, certainly. This is trainable, but you have to pull yourself through the information because your eyes are attracted to motion, right? If you're a hunter-gatherer, if the bush next to you moves, you have to look because that's your survival. Number one, that could be lunch. Or number two, you could be lunch, right? Either way. So your eyes are attracted to motion. So when you're using a visual pacer, a highlighter, a mouse on a computer, a pen, your finger, whatever it is, your eyes are being pulled through the information as opposed to your attention being pulled apart. Using your finger will help you improve your speed. The opposite is regression. Regression is back skipping, rereading words. Some people read whole lines by accident. And it's your waste of a lot of time. You're not going to back-skip when you're pulling your finger across the page or using a highlighter, a pen, or whatever. The other thing that could help you get more out of it is asking, just how we prompt AI. We're not prompting our mind with useful questions. If you're reading something and asking yourself questions like, how can I use this? How does this relate to what I know? When will I use this? So like if I finish the first section, then ask a question that I'm hoping to get answered in the second section? Yeah. The things that we let in, there's like a little gatekeeper called your reticular activating system, but RAS, it's engaged by what's important to you. And usually what directs that spotlight are the questions you're asking.
